text:
Yes, he said, I wrote that. It was so long ago; it was one night, the poplars outside my window were rustling so when I wrote it. No, are you really putting it away again? Thank you! You put it away again. Oh! he exclaimed, enraptured, and his voice was quite low, just think that you are sitting no farther away than this. I feel your arm against mine; a warmth radiates from you. Many a time, when I was alone and thought of you, I froze with emotion; but now I am warm. The last time I was home you were lovely then too; but you are lovelier now. It is the eyes and the eyebrows, your smile—no, I do not know, it is everything, everything about you.

She smiled and looked at him with half-closed eyes; beneath the long lashes there was a dark blue shadow. She had a warm glow. She seemed to be prey to the highest joy and reached toward him with her hand in an unconscious movement.

Thank you! she said.

No, Victoria, do not thank me, he answered. His whole soul streamed toward her, and he wanted to say more, say more; it became confused outbursts, he was as though intoxicated. Yes, but Victoria, if you are a little fond of me.... I do not know, but say that you are, even if it is not so. Please. Oh, I should promise you to become something, become a great deal, almost an unheard-of amount. You have no idea what I could become; I ponder it sometimes and know that I am utterly full of deeds not yet done. Many a time it pours out of me; at night I pace up and down the floor of my room because I am full of visions. There is a man in the room next door; he cannot sleep, he knocks on the wall. When morning dawns he comes in to me and is furious. It does not matter, I do not care about him; for by then I have thought of you for so long that I feel you are with me. I go to the window and sing; it is beginning to grow a little light, the poplars rustle outside. Good night! I say to the day. It is meant for you. Now she is sleeping, I think, good night, God bless her! Then I lie down. So it goes, evening after evening. But I never believed that you were as lovely as you are. Now I will remember you like this when you leave; as you are now. I will remember you so clearly....

Are you not coming home?

No. I am not finished. Yes, I am coming. I am leaving now. I am not finished, but I will do all manner of things. Do you sometimes wander in the garden at home now? Do you ever go out in the evening? I could see you, I could perhaps have the chance to greet you; it is not for anything else. But if you are a little fond of me, if you can tolerate me, endure me, then say.... Grant me that joy.... Do you know, there is a palm that blossoms only once in its life, and yet it lives to be seventy years old, the talipot palm. But it blossoms only once. I am blossoming now. Yes, I will get some money and go home. I shall sell what I have written; you see, I am writing a large book, and I shall sell it now, at once tomorrow, everything I have finished. I shall get a good deal for it. Would you then want me to come home?

a.
Thank you, thank you! Forgive me if I hope too much, believe too much; it is so lovely to believe an extraordinary amount. This is the happiest day I have lived....

He took off his hat and laid it beside him.

Victoria looked around; a lady was coming down the street, and farther up there was a woman with a basket. Victoria grew uneasy; she reached for her watch.

Must you go now? he asked. Say something before you go, let me hear your.... I love you, and I am saying it now. Whether I.... will depend on your answer. You have such absolute power over me. What is your answer?

Pause.

He lowers his head.
No, do not say it! he begged.

Not here, she answered. I shall do it down there.

They walked on.

People say that you are going to marry the little girl, the girl, the one you rescued; what is her name?

Camilla, do you mean?

Camilla Seier. People say that you are going to marry her.

Is that so. Why do you ask? She is not grown up. I have been to her home; it is so large and rich, a palace like your own; I have been there many times. No, she is not grown up.

She is fifteen years old. I have met her; we have spent time together. I became very fond of her. How lovely she is!

I am not going to marry her, he said.

Oh, you are not.

He looked at her. A twitch passed over his face.

But why are you saying this now? Do you wish to direct my attention to someone else?

She walked on with rapid steps and did not answer. They were outside the chamberlain’s house. She took his hand and pulled him through the gateway and up the stairs.

I am not going in, he said, half astonished.

She pressed the bell; she turned toward him, and her breast heaved.

I love you, she said. Do you understand that? It is you I love.

Suddenly she pulled him quickly down the stairs again, three, four steps, threw her arms around him, and kissed him. She trembled against him.

It is you I love, she said.

The entrance door opened above. She tore herself free and hurried up the stairs.

IV

It is drawing toward morning; day is dawning, a bluish, trembling September morning.

The poplars in the garden murmur softly. A window opens; a man leans out of it and hums. He has no coat on; he looks out into the world like an undressed madman who tonight has drunk himself drunk on happiness.

He suddenly turns away from the window and looks toward his door; someone has knocked. He calls: Come in! A man enters.

Good morning! he says to the man entering.
He is an elderly man; he is pale and furious, and he carries a lamp because it is not yet quite light.

Once again I must ask you, Mr. Møller, Mr. Johannes Møller, whether you consider this reasonable, the man stammers bitterly.

No, Johannes answers, you are right. I have written something; it came to me so readily; look, I have written all this, I have been fortunate tonight. But now I am finished. I opened the window and sang a little.

You bellowed, the man says. It is the loudest singing I have ever heard, do you understand? And it is still the middle of the night.

Johannes grabs at his papers on the table and takes a handful of large and small sheets.

Look here! he cries. I tell you, it has never gone so well for me. It was like one long flash of lightning. I once saw a bolt of lightning that followed a telegraph wire; God help you, it looked like a sheet of fire. That is how it has poured through me tonight. What am I to do? I do not think you will hold anything against me any longer when you hear how matters stand. I sat here and wrote, do you hear, I did not move; I remembered you and kept quiet. Then comes the moment when I no longer remember it; my chest was about to burst; perhaps I rose then, perhaps I also rose once more in the course of the night and walked around the floor a few times. I was so happy.
